entry.title: Backpropagation, one scalar at a time

link.title: Backpropagation, one scalar at a time

entry.content:
loss.backward() hides a small amount of calculus. I wanted to write that calculus out without memorising any matrix-calculus identities, so this post is the derivation from my notes. The idea is to stop looking at tensors and treat every tensor entry as a separate scalar variable. The only tool left is the ordinary chain rule, and formulas like \(g W^T\) and \(x^T g\) come out at the end.

From layers to one large graph

A deep architecture is a sequence of simple layers, with each layer’s output wired into the next layer’s input. Joining them gives one large computational graph of tensors that ends in the scalar loss. It is a directed acyclic graph (DAG): values only flow forward, so nothing depends on itself.

Each edge comes with a local equation, the derivative of its output with respect to its input. It only involves that one operation and knows nothing about the rest of the network.

Backpropagation needs exactly these two things:

  1. The DAG, which says what feeds what, and so which paths lead to the loss and in what order to visit them.
  2. The local derivative on every edge.

Given those, the chain rule does the rest. Each tensor is also a grid of entries, so underneath this graph sits an even larger DAG of scalars, and that is the level where the chain rule is simplest to write.

The graph is made of scalars

Draw the computation graph at its finest level. Every entry of every input, parameter and intermediate tensor is a node, and the last node is a single scalar, the loss \(\mathcal{L}\).

For any node \(v\), write \(\bar{v}\) for the derivative of the loss with respect to it. So \(\bar{y} = \partial \mathcal{L} / \partial y\), and at the end of the graph \(\bar{\mathcal{L}} = \partial \mathcal{L} / \partial \mathcal{L} = 1\).

The bar of any node comes from the chain rule. A node \(v\) can only affect the loss through the nodes it feeds directly, so its derivative is a sum over those children, each term being the child’s own bar times the local derivative on the edge:

\[\bar{v} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial v} = \sum_{c \,\in\, \text{children}(v)} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial c} \cdot \frac{\partial c}{\partial v} = \sum_{c \,\in\, \text{children}(v)} \bar{c} \cdot \frac{\partial c}{\partial v}\]

This recursion is the chain rule applied at every node of the DAG, and that is all backpropagation is. To evaluate it at \(v\) we need \(\bar{c}\) for every child first, so we start at the loss, where \(\bar{\mathcal{L}} = 1\), and visit the nodes in reverse order. Written out in full, the chain rule is a sum over every path from \(v\) to the loss of the product of the edge derivatives along that path. The recursion gives the same number but reuses each \(\bar{c}\) instead of walking every path separately. Each edge is used once, so the backward pass costs about as much as the forward pass.

I’ll name directions by how the gradient travels. It starts at the loss, so for any layer the output side is upstream and the input side is downstream.

Index notation

For a tensor \(A\) of shape \((I, J)\), \(A_{ij}\) is one element, and a matrix product is a contraction over the shared index:

\[(A \cdot B)_{ij} = \sum_k A_{ik} B_{kj}\]

Every entry is its own independent variable, so the derivative of one entry with respect to another is 1 if they are the same entry and 0 otherwise:

\[\frac{\partial y_{b'j'}}{\partial y_{bj}} = \delta_{bb'}\delta_{jj'}, \qquad \frac{\partial W_{i'j'}}{\partial W_{ij}} = \delta_{ii'}\delta_{jj'}, \qquad \frac{\partial B_{j'}}{\partial B_{j}} = \delta_{jj'}\]

These deltas are what make the sums collapse. Any sum over a primed index that contains a delta on that index has only one surviving term.

A gradient has the same shape as the tensor it is taken against. The one we will pass between layers gets its own letter, \(g\), which is the bar of a layer’s output:

\[g = \bar{y} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y}, \qquad g_{bj} = \bar{y}_{bj} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y_{bj}}\]

The linear layer

The graph is too large to reason about node by node, so we group nodes into layers. A layer receives \(g\) from upstream and has to produce two things: the gradient for its input, to send downstream, and the gradients for its own parameters.

The forward pass, in matrix form and by index, with \(b\) running over the batch:

\[y = xW + B, \qquad y_{bj} = \sum_{i'} x_{bi'} W_{i'j} + B_j\]

Gradient for the input

Differentiating \(y_{bj}\) by an input entry in the same batch row:

\[\frac{\partial y_{bj}}{\partial x_{bi}} = \sum_{i'} \delta_{ii'} W_{i'j} = W_{ij}\]

Different batch rows do not interact, so the chain rule only sums over the outputs \(j\):

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_{bi}} = \sum_j \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y_{bj}} \frac{\partial y_{bj}}{\partial x_{bi}} = \sum_j g_{bj} W_{ij} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{\bar{x} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = g W^T}\]

The shapes check: \((N, J) \cdot (J, I) = (N, I)\). This is what the layer sends downstream, and the next layer down receives it as its own \(g\).

Gradient for the weights

Here the indices need care. Fix the weight \(W_{ij}\) we are differentiating against, and use primes for the entries of \(y\) that might depend on it. Every batch row and every output is a candidate, so the chain rule sums over both:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_{ij}} = \sum_{b, j'} g_{bj'} \frac{\partial y_{bj'}}{\partial W_{ij}}\]

The local derivative uses the deltas from above, and the bias does not depend on \(W\):

\[\frac{\partial y_{bj'}}{\partial W_{ij}} = \sum_{i'} x_{bi'} \frac{\partial W_{i'j'}}{\partial W_{ij}} + \frac{\partial B_{j'}}{\partial W_{ij}} = \sum_{i'} x_{bi'} \delta_{ii'} \delta_{jj'} + 0 = x_{bi} \delta_{jj'}\]

Substituting, the \(j'\) sum collapses and only the batch sum is left:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_{ij}} = \sum_b x_{bi}\, g_{bj} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{\bar{W} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W} = x^T g}\]

Again the shapes check: \((I, N) \cdot (N, J) = (I, J)\). The input \(x\) appears in this result, and it belongs to the forward pass. So the layer has to cache \(x\) on the way forward to be able to compute its weight gradient on the way back.

Gradient for the bias

\(B_j\) enters each \(y_{bj'}\) additively, so \(\partial y_{bj'} / \partial B_j = \delta_{jj'}\), and

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial B_j} = \sum_{b, j'} g_{bj'} \delta_{jj'} = \sum_b g_{bj} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{\bar{B} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial B} = \sum_b g}\]

Nothing needs caching here. The bias gradient is just the upstream gradient summed over the batch.

Where each sum comes from

The form of each result is decided by one question: if I nudge this variable, which entries of \(y\) move?

The activation layer

An activation has no parameters and applies a scalar function \(f\) to each entry, so \(x\) and \(y\) have the same shape:

\[y_{bj} = f(x_{bj})\]

For the local derivative, take any output entry against any input entry:

\[\frac{\partial y_{b'j'}}{\partial x_{bj}} = f'(x_{b'j'}) \frac{\partial x_{b'j'}}{\partial x_{bj}} = f'(x_{bj})\, \delta_{bb'} \delta_{jj'}\]

Only \(y_{bj}\) is affected by \(x_{bj}\). The chain rule’s sum over \(b', j'\) has one surviving term:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_{bj}} = \sum_{b', j'} g_{b'j'} \frac{\partial y_{b'j'}}{\partial x_{bj}} = g_{bj} f'(x_{bj}) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{\bar{x} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = g \odot f'(x)}\]

where \(\odot\) is the element-wise product. \(f'\) is evaluated at the input, so this layer also needs its cached \(x\).

All the rules

Layer Forward Sent downstream, \(\bar{x}\) Parameter gradients Cached
Linear \(y = xW + B\) \(g W^T\) \(\bar{W} = x^T g\), \(\bar{B} = \textstyle\sum_b g\) \(x\)
Activation \(y = f(x)\) \(g \odot f'(x)\) none \(x\)

A network is a chain of these. The forward pass fills the caches, the loss produces the first \(g\), and each layer in reverse order converts the \(g\) it receives into the \(g\) for the layer below it.

The rules translate almost symbol for symbol:

import numpy as np

class Linear:
    def __init__(self, I, J):
        self.W = np.random.randn(I, J)
        self.B = np.random.randn(J)

    def forward(self, x):                # x: (N, I)
        self.x = x                       # needed later for dW
        return x @ self.W + self.B       # y: (N, J)

    def backward(self, g):               # g = dL/dy: (N, J)
        self.dW = self.x.T @ g           # (I, J)
        self.dB = g.sum(axis=0)          # (J)
        return g @ self.W.T              # dL/dx: (N, I)

class Activation:
    def __init__(self, f, df):
        self.f, self.df = f, df

    def forward(self, x):
        self.x = x                       # f' is evaluated at the input
        return self.f(x)

    def backward(self, g):
        return g * self.df(self.x)       # element-wise

I checked this against central finite differences on a Linear, tanh, Linear network with a squared-error loss. Over every entry of the input, weights and biases, the largest disagreement with the analytic gradient was about \(4 \times 10^{-9}\).

What never gets built

The full Jacobian \(\partial y / \partial x\) of a linear layer is a tensor of shape \((N, J, N, I)\). Backpropagation never constructs it. Each layer only computes the product of \(g\) with that Jacobian, and the index work above shows the product is one matrix multiply, or one element-wise multiply. The memory cost is the caches.

This is also what an autograd engine does. It records the operations during the forward pass, and for each operation it holds a rule of exactly this form: given the gradient of the output, return the gradient of the inputs. My Java MLP from school has the same backward pass, written by hand for one architecture. Autograd generalises it to any graph of operations that have such a rule.
entry.summary: Deriving the gradient rules for linear and activation layers from the plain chain rule, treating every tensor entry as its own variable.

entry.title: From expected utility to the belief MDP

link.title: From expected utility to the belief MDP

entry.content:
Influence diagrams, MDPs and POMDPs are usually taught as three separate topics. In my notes they are one equation, maximum expected utility, applied with different answers to a single question: what does the agent know at the moment it decides? This post follows that equation from a single decision to the belief MDP, then shows what changes when the model is unknown.

One principle

An agent takes actions in a probabilistic environment and gets rewards. Outcomes have utility.

One piece of notation first, because it appears everywhere below. An expectation is only a weighted sum: for any function \(f\) and whatever we are conditioning on,

\[E[f(x) \mid \ldots] = \sum_x P(x \mid \ldots)\, f(x)\]

Expected utility is this with \(f = U\) and \(x\) the outcome. Given an action \(a\) and evidence \(e\):

\[EU(a \mid e) = E[U \mid a, e] = \sum_{\text{outcomes}} P(\text{outcome} \mid a, e)\; U(\text{outcome})\]

The principle of maximum expected utility (MEU) says to pick the action that maximises this:

\[a^* = \arg\max_a EU(a \mid e), \qquad MEU[e] = \max_a EU(a \mid e)\]

Where outcomes have utility, situations have value. A situation is what the agent knows or believes, and its value is the expected utility it can still collect from there onwards. For a sequence of rewards, utility is either the plain sum over an episode, or a discounted sum:

\[U = \sum_{t=0}^{T} r_t \qquad\text{or}\qquad U = \sum_t \gamma^t r_t\]

The three models differ only in what fills the slots:

Model Evidence the agent holds Outcome summed over
Influence diagram \(e\), about a state \(s\) \(s\)
MDP the state \(s\) itself next state \(s'\)
POMDP the history \(h\) \(s, s', o\)

As in other probabilistic graphical models, everything below uses the same two operations: \(\oplus\) is a sum over unobserved variables, or a max at a decision, and \(\otimes\) is the product of local factors.

One decision: influence diagrams

Take one timestep, \(T = 1\). The action does not move the world, so \(s' = s\), and \(s\) may not be fully observable.

\[EU(a \mid e) = \sum_s P(s \mid a, e)\, U(s, a) = \sum_s P(s \mid e)\, U(s, a)\]

The second step uses \(s \perp a \mid e\): the action is chosen from the evidence alone, so it says nothing further about the state. If the transition is deterministic, \(\text{Result}(s, a) = s'\), then a utility on outcomes and a utility on state-action pairs are the same thing, \(U(s') = U(s, a)\).

The general formula

The same recipe works for any influence diagram, in three steps. Write \(\text{pa}(X)\) for the parents of a node \(X\).

1. Chain the joint. The joint distribution of all chance variables is the product of one local factor per chance node, each given its parents. Decisions appear only as fixed inputs to those factors:

\[P(\text{chance vars} \mid \text{decisions}) = \prod_i P(X_i \mid \text{pa}(X_i))\]

2. Take the expectation. Expected utility is the \(E[f(x) \mid \ldots]\) sum from earlier, with \(x\) being all the chance variables and \(f\) being the utility:

\[EU(\text{decisions}) = E[U \mid \text{decisions}] = \sum_{\text{chance vars}} \prod_i P(X_i \mid \text{pa}(X_i))\; U(\text{pa}(U))\]

3. Put each max where its decision happens. If no decision observes anything first, one max goes outside: \(MEU = \max_{\text{decisions}} EU\), and \(\arg\max\) gives the decisions themselves. If decisions do observe chance variables, order everything in time. Let \(C_0\) be the variables known before decision \(d_1\), \(C_1\) those revealed between \(d_1\) and \(d_2\), and \(C_n\) those never seen before the last decision. Assuming each decision remembers everything before it:

\[MEU = \underbrace{\sum_{C_0} \max_{d_1} \sum_{C_1} \cdots \max_{d_n} \sum_{C_n}}_{\text{sums and maxes in time order}}\; \underbrace{\prod_i P(X_i \mid \text{pa}(X_i))}_{\text{chained joint}}\; \underbrace{U(\text{pa}(U))}_{\text{utility}}\]

The order is what matters. A sum outside a max is a variable that decision can see, so the choice may depend on it. A sum inside a max is still unknown when the decision is made, so the decision can only average over it.

For the diagram above, the chained joint is \(P(s)\,P(e \mid s)\), and \(e\) is seen before \(a\) while \(s\) is not, so the order is \(\sum_e \max_a \sum_s\):

\[\begin{aligned} MEU &= \sum_e \max_a \sum_s P(s)\, P(e \mid s)\, U(s, a) \\ &= \sum_e P(e) \max_a \sum_s P(s \mid e)\, U(s, a) \\ &= \sum_e P(e)\, MEU[e] \end{aligned}\]

The sequential models below have this same form, a repeating \(\max_{a_0} \sum_{s_1} \max_{a_1} \sum_{s_2} \cdots\), and the Bellman equation is that nesting written as a recursion.

Full observability: the MDP

An MDP is \(\langle S, A, T, R \rangle\) with transition model \(T(s, a, s') = P(s' \mid s, a)\). Start from MEU, with the expected utility of an action now called \(Q\):

\[EU(a \mid e) = \sum_{s, s'} P(s, s' \mid a, e)\, U(s, a, s') = \sum_{s, s'} P(s \mid s', a, e)\, P(s' \mid a, e)\, U(s, a, s')\]

Full observability means the evidence names the state exactly. So \(P(s \mid s', a, e)\) is 1 for that state and 0 for every other, and the sum over \(s\) disappears.

Now the utility. The value \(V(s)\) is the expected utility from \(s\) onwards if the agent acts optimally, which makes it \(MEU[s]\) for the whole remaining sequence:

\[V(s) = \max_\pi E\Big[ \sum_t \gamma^t r_t \;\Big|\; s_0 = s, \pi \Big]\]

\(Q(s, a)\) is the same expected utility with the first action fixed to \(a\), so \(Q(s, a) = EU(a \mid s)\). The utility of an outcome \(s'\) is therefore the immediate reward plus the expected utility from \(s'\) onwards:

\[U(s, a, s') = R(s, a, s') + \gamma V(s')\]

Substituting gives the action value, and acting by MEU gives the state value. Together they are the Bellman equation:

\[Q(s, a) = \sum_{s'} T(s, a, s') \big[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma V(s') \big], \qquad V(s) = \max_a Q(s, a)\]

Splitting the bracket shows the two parts of an action’s value, the expected immediate return and the expected future return, with \(R(s, a) = \sum_{s'} T(s, a, s') R(s, a, s')\):

\[Q(s, a) = R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s, a, s')\, V(s')\]

Solving it

Value iteration turns the Bellman equation into an update, starting from any assumed \(V_0\):

\[V_{k+1}(s) = \max_a Q_k(s, a)\]

Policy iteration alternates two steps. A policy \(\pi(a \mid s)\) is a distribution over actions, or a single action \(\pi(s)\) if deterministic. Policy evaluation computes its value:

\[V^\pi_{k+1}(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s'} T(s, a, s') \big[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma V^\pi_k(s') \big]\]

With no max in it, this is a linear system in \(V^\pi\), which can be solved directly or approximated with a few sweeps. Policy improvement then applies MEU, \(\pi'(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s, a)\), and we stop when \(\pi' = \pi\).

Both methods solve for \(Q\) through \(V\) and extract \(\pi\) by MEU. In an MDP a deterministic policy is enough, because a max is never smaller than an average:

\[\max_a Q(s, a) \;\geq\; \sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\, Q(s, a)\]

Hidden state: the POMDP

A POMDP \(\langle S, A, T, R, O \rangle\) removes direct access to \(s\). Actions now also produce observations, through \(O(o, s', a) = P(o \mid s', a)\), and the outcome of a step is the pair \((s', o)\).

The evidence is now the history of everything the agent has done and seen:

\[h_t = (a_0, o_1, \ldots, a_{t-1}, o_t), \qquad h' = \langle h, a, o \rangle\]

Each history is a new situation, and histories have value the way states do in an MDP. The derivations below lean on three independences read straight from the model:

  • \(o \perp s, h \mid s', a\), which is the definition of \(O\).
  • \(s' \perp h \mid s, a\), which is the definition of \(T\).
  • \(s \perp a \mid h\), because the action is chosen from the history alone.

Histories form an MDP

The state only matters through what the history says about it, so \(\langle H, A, T, R \rangle\) is an MDP with \(R(h, a) = \sum_s P(s \mid h) R(s, a)\). Its transition reduces to the probability of the next observation, since \(P(A, B \mid A) = P(B \mid A)\) gives \(T(h, a, h') = P(\langle h, a, o \rangle \mid h, a) = P(o \mid h, a)\). Expanding that over the hidden states:

\[\begin{aligned} P(o \mid h, a) &= \sum_{s, s'} P(o \mid s, s', h, a)\, P(s, s' \mid h, a) \\ &= \sum_{s, s'} P(o \mid s', a)\, P(s' \mid s, h, a)\, P(s \mid h, a) \\ &= \sum_s P(s \mid h) \sum_{s'} O(o, s', a)\, T(s, a, s') \end{aligned}\]

This MDP is correct but unusable. The number of histories at depth \(T\) is \((\lvert A \rvert \lvert O \rvert)^T\), exponential in the horizon, and the number of policies over that tree is doubly exponential.

The Q function over histories

Apply MEU with \(e = h\). Only the history has value here, since it is all the agent knows, so the utility of an outcome is \(R(s, a, s') + \gamma V(h, a, o)\):

\[\begin{aligned} Q(h, a) &= \sum_{s, s', o} P(s, s', o \mid a, h) \big[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma V(h, a, o) \big] \\ &= \sum_{s, s', o} P(o \mid s', a)\, P(s' \mid s, a)\, P(s \mid h) \big[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma V(h, a, o) \big] \\ &= \sum_s P(s \mid h) \sum_{s'} T(s, a, s') \sum_o O(o, s', a) \big[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma V(h, a, o) \big] \end{aligned}\]

Since \(\sum_o O(o, s', a) = 1\), the reward term loses its sum over \(o\), and \(Q\) splits as \(Q(h, a) = R(h, a) + F(h, a)\) with

\[R(h, a) = \sum_s P(s \mid h) \sum_{s'} T(s, a, s')\, R(s, a, s')\] \[F(h, a) = \gamma \sum_o V(h, a, o) \sum_s P(s \mid h) \sum_{s'} O(o, s', a)\, T(s, a, s')\]

Introducing the belief

Look at where \(h\) appears. Apart from \(V(h, a, o)\), it is only ever inside \(P(s \mid h)\). So define the belief and its successor:

\[b(s) = P(s \mid h), \qquad b'(s') = P(s' \mid h'), \quad h' = \langle h, a, o \rangle\]

\(R(h, a)\) uses \(h\) only through \(b\), so \(R(h, a) \triangleq R(b, a)\), where \(\triangleq\) means the history-indexed quantity is determined by the belief. \(F\) still contains \(V(h, a, o) = V(h')\). To remove it we need two things: a way to compute \(b'\) without the history, and a proof that \(V\) depends on the history only through the belief.

The belief update

Apply Bayes’ rule to the new observation, then the independences:

\[\begin{aligned} b'(s') = P(s' \mid h, a, o) &= \frac{P(s', o \mid h, a)}{P(o \mid h, a)} = \frac{P(o \mid s', a)\, P(s' \mid h, a)}{P(o \mid h, a)} \\ &= \frac{P(o \mid s', a)}{P(o \mid h, a)} \sum_s P(s' \mid s, h, a)\, P(s \mid h, a) \\ &= \frac{P(o \mid s', a)}{P(o \mid h, a)} \sum_s T(s, a, s')\, b(s) \end{aligned}\]

The denominator is the transition we already derived, which only needs \(b\):

\[P(o \mid h, a) = \sum_{s, s'} b(s)\, O(o, s', a)\, T(s, a, s') \triangleq P(o \mid b, a)\]

It is only a normalising constant, so the update is

\[\boxed{\, b'(s') = \frac{O(o, s', a) \sum_s T(s, a, s')\, b(s)}{\sum_{s'} O(o, s', a) \sum_s T(s, a, s')\, b(s)} \,}\]

It predicts the state forward through \(T\), reweights by how well each state explains the observation, and normalises. It needs only \((b, a, o)\).

Proof that the belief is sufficient

We want \(V(h) \triangleq V(b)\), by induction backwards from the last stage. Recall \(V(h) = \max_a Q(h, a)\).

Base case, \(t = T - 1\). No further action is allowed, so there is no future term:

\[Q(h, a) = R(h, a) + 0 = R(b, a) \triangleq Q(b, a) \quad\Rightarrow\quad V(h) \triangleq V(b)\]

Inductive step. Assume \(V(h') = V(b')\) at time \(t+1\) and prove it at \(t\):

\[\begin{aligned} V(h) &= \max_a \Big[ R(b, a) + \gamma \sum_o V(h') \sum_s b(s) \sum_{s'} O(o, s', a)\, T(s, a, s') \Big] \\ &= \max_a \Big[ R(b, a) + \gamma \sum_o V(b') \sum_s b(s) \sum_{s'} O(o, s', a)\, T(s, a, s') \Big] \triangleq V(b) \end{aligned}\]

Because \(b'\) is a function of \((b, a, o)\), the whole expression depends on \(h\) only through \(b\). The same argument without the max gives \(Q(h, a) \triangleq Q(b, a)\). The belief is a sufficient statistic of the history for acting optimally.

The belief MDP

So we can throw away histories and write a Bellman equation directly over beliefs:

\[Q(b, a) = R(b, a) + \gamma \sum_o P(o \mid b, a)\, V(b'), \qquad V(b) = \max_a Q(b, a)\] \[R(b, a) = \sum_{s, s'} b(s)\, T(s, a, s')\, R(s, a, s')\]

It has the same shape as the MDP backup, with the belief as the state and the observation as the source of randomness. It also has far fewer distinct reachable situations, because many histories lead to the same belief, so the tree folds into something closer to a DAG.

The catch is that \(b\) is continuous, so we cannot brute-force a table over it.

Solving it

Two approximations reuse the solution of the underlying MDP \(\langle S, A, T, R \rangle\), giving \(V(s)\), \(Q(s, a)\) and \(\pi(s)\), while tracking \(b' = \text{update}(b, a, o)\) at run time:

  • Most likely state: \(s_{ML} = \arg\max_s b(s)\), then \(\pi(b) = \pi(s_{ML})\).
  • QMDP: \(Q(b, a) = \sum_s b(s) Q(s, a)\), then \(\pi(b) = \arg\max_a Q(b, a)\).

Both act as if the uncertainty will be gone after the current step, so neither will take an action purely to gain information.

The exact solution uses the structure of \(V\). A plan with \(k\) steps to go has an expected reward from each state, which is a vector \(\alpha(s)\). With one step to go, \(\alpha(s) = R(s, a)\). Let \(\Gamma_k\) be the finite set of such plans. Then

\[V_k(b) = \max_{\alpha \in \Gamma_k} \sum_s \alpha(s)\, b(s)\]

This form survives a backup because of a cancellation. In \(Q(b, a)\), the value \(V(b')\) is multiplied by \(P(o \mid b, a)\), which is exactly the denominator of the belief update:

\[P(o \mid b, a) \sum_{s'} \alpha(s')\, b'(s') = \sum_{s'} \alpha(s')\, O(o, s', a) \sum_s T(s, a, s')\, b(s)\]

The right side is linear in \(b\), so each new plan is again a linear function of the belief, and value iteration can run on the sets \(\Gamma_k\) until it converges to within \(\epsilon\). Each plan is a straight line over beliefs, and the max switches between lines in different regions of \(b\). That makes \(V\) piecewise linear and convex (PWLC).

Without the model: reinforcement learning

Now go back to the fully observable \(\langle S, A, T, R \rangle\), but suppose the tables \(T\) and \(R\) are unknown. All we have is experience: tuples of \(s, a, r, s'\) and sometimes \(a'\).

Two distinctions organise the methods. Passive learning estimates the value \(V^\pi\) of a given policy, and active learning looks for \(\pi^*, Q^*, V^*\). Model-based methods estimate \(T\) and \(R\) and then solve the MDP (adaptive dynamic programming), and model-free methods go straight for \(Q^*, V^*\) or \(\pi^*\). The target matters as well: getting a policy from \(V\) needs \(T\) for the one-step lookahead, but getting one from \(Q\) does not.

The model-free move is to replace the expectation in the Bellman backup by a single sample:

\[\underbrace{\sum_{s'} T(s, a, s') \big[ R(s, a, s') + \gamma V(s') \big]}_{\text{model}} \;\longrightarrow\; \underbrace{r + \gamma V(s')}_{\text{sample, bootstrapped}}\]

Each algorithm then nudges its estimate towards that sample by a step size \(\alpha\) (unrelated to the \(\alpha\)-vectors above). The bracketed difference is the temporal-difference error.

TD learning updates after each transition \((s, a, r, s')\). It bootstraps on its own estimate, so it is biased.

\[V^\pi(s) \leftarrow V^\pi(s) + \alpha \big[ r + \gamma V^\pi(s') - V^\pi(s) \big]\]

Monte Carlo does not bootstrap. It runs trajectories to the end and averages the observed returns \(G_t\), which is unbiased but needs much more data.

Q-learning also updates after \((s, a, r, s')\). The max makes it off-policy: it learns the greedy values whatever the agent actually did.

\[Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \big[ r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a) \big]\]

Sarsa waits for the next action too, using \((s, a, r, s', a')\). It is on-policy and converges to \(Q^\pi\), so \(\pi\) has to improve along the way to reach \(\pi^*\).

\[Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \big[ r + \gamma Q(s', a') - Q(s, a) \big]\]

Off-policy learning is the more attractive idea, but Sarsa tends to be more stable and more realistic about what the agent will actually do.

Since the agent’s own actions determine its data, it has to explore:

  • \(\epsilon\)-greedy takes the greedy action with probability \(1 - \epsilon\) and a random one otherwise.
  • R-MAX is optimistic. Until \((s, a)\) has been tried \(m\) times, it assumes \(T(s, a, s') = \delta_{ss'}\) and \(R(s, a) = R_{\max}\). After that it switches to the maximum-likelihood estimates \(\hat{T}(s, a, s') = N(s, a, s') / N(s, a)\) and the mean observed reward.
  • UCB1 adds a bonus for rarely tried actions: \(a_t = \arg\max_a \big[ \hat{Q}(a) + c \sqrt{\ln N / N_a} \big]\).

When the tables are too large, \(Q\) or \(V\) become deep networks, trained by the backward pass from my backprop post. This introduces the deadly triad: bootstrapping, off-policy learning and function approximation, which together can make the estimates diverge. A different route parametrises the policy itself, \(\pi(a \mid s; \omega)\), and follows the gradient of the return, as in REINFORCE:

\[\omega_{t+1} = \omega_t + \alpha \gamma^t G_t \nabla_\omega \log \pi(a_t \mid s_t; \omega_t)\]

Actor-critic methods combine the two, with a learned value function supporting a learned policy.

entry.title: InferQ: can a database simulate a quantum computer?

link.title: InferQ: can a database simulate a quantum computer?

entry.content:
Simulating a quantum circuit classically usually means tracking a state vector or tensor network directly, with a purpose-built simulator like Qiskit Aer doing the heavy lifting. But there’s a less obvious angle: circuit simulation is, at its core, a sequence of tensor contractions — and tensor contraction can be expressed as a join-and-aggregate SQL query. Represent two tensors as rows of (i, k, val) and (k, j, val), join them on the shared index k, multiply, and sum out k:

-- matrix multiplication w = A x B, expressed as a join-and-aggregate query
SELECT A.i, B.j, SUM(A.val * B.val) AS w_ij
FROM A JOIN B ON A.k = B.k
GROUP BY A.i, B.j;

That’s the whole trick — applying a gate to a quantum state is just this pattern, over and over. So: could a general-purpose relational database, with decades of engineering behind query optimization and out-of-core memory management, be a competitive quantum simulator?

Prior work showed isolated, striking results in this direction — DuckDB simulating GHZ-state preparation out to millions of qubits under a tight memory budget. But those results were on a narrow set of highly structured circuits, and it wasn’t clear when this approach generalizes versus when it falls apart (the same study found a dense circuit like the Quantum Fourier Transform tops out at just 14 qubits under identical conditions).

InferQ, published with Andrei Ilinescu and Rihan Hai at SIGMOD 2027, is a benchmark built to answer that question systematically rather than case-by-case. It:

  • Generates general, compositional circuits by assembling subcircuits from a library of templates, rather than restricting to a handful of textbook circuit families.
  • Compiles every circuit into an RDBMS-ready SQL workload, so the same circuit can be handed directly to PostgreSQL, SQLite, DuckDB, or Umbra.
  • Extracts circuit and query features — static, graph-structural, SQL-level, and dynamic — so a workload can be characterized numerically, not just by eyeballing the circuit diagram.
  • Releases a dataset of 202,975 generated circuits with all their features, plus a web-based viewer for searching, filtering, and downloading circuits.

Running this benchmark across four RDBMS engines and Qiskit Aer, we found RDBMSs achieve better peak memory usage than Aer on more than half of the generated circuits — the database approach isn’t a narrow party trick, it’s broadly competitive on memory. More interesting, though: using InferQ’s extracted features, simple linear and tree-based models can predict which engine will be faster or more memory-efficient for a given circuit with up to 95.6% (runtime) and 97.4% (memory) accuracy. That turns “should I simulate this circuit with a database or a dedicated simulator” from a case-by-case guess into a data-driven, learned decision — a small step toward automatic, workload-aware simulator selection.

This sits right alongside my earlier work on Matrix Product State simulation: both are ultimately about choosing the right computational substrate for a given circuit’s structure, whether that’s a tensor network or a relational database.

Paper, abstract, and PDF are on the publications page (Ilinescu et al., 2026).
entry.summary: A benchmark for running quantum circuit simulation as SQL, and when it actually beats Qiskit.

entry.title: QEC lake: a data lake for quantum error correction

link.title: QEC lake: a data lake for quantum error correction

entry.content:
Quantum error correction (QEC) is what makes a fault-tolerant quantum computer possible: physical qubits are noisy, so QEC codes spread logical information across many physical qubits and use repeated syndrome measurements to detect and correct errors. Decoding — turning a stream of noisy syndrome measurements into “which qubits flipped” — is increasingly done with AI models rather than hand-designed algorithms, because learned decoders can adapt to the messy, correlated noise of real hardware better than classical decoders can.

The catch: training a good decoder needs a lot of QEC data, and that data is a mess. Every code family (surface codes, color codes, …) and every hardware platform emits data in its own schema. Datasets are scattered across incompatible repositories, often undocumented, and rarely large enough on their own. Comparing two decoders fairly is hard when they were never trained or evaluated on comparable data in the first place.

QEC lake, the paper Max de Groot, Andrei Ilinescu, Aditya Shankar, Yuandou Wang, Wenbo Sun, Floris Geerts, Rihan Hai and I demoed at VLDB 2026, is a domain-specific data lake built to fix exactly this. It:

  • Continuously crawls and refreshes open QEC datasets from across code families and hardware platforms into one place.
  • Generates new data — user-configurable simulated circuits, and synthetic variants derived from real hardware data — to fill in the gaps where real data is scarce.
  • Manages metadata for discovery, so a researcher can actually find the subset of data relevant to their code family, distance, and noise model instead of digging through disconnected repos.
  • Prepares model-ready inputs, converting heterogeneous raw data into the tabular formats tree-based models and tabular foundation models expect, plus an AI-assisted natural-language interface for exploring the data.

At the VLDB demo, attendees ingested sources, generated new datasets on the spot, explored them through structured and natural-language queries, and exported model-ready training data — the full pipeline from “scattered QEC data” to “something a decoder can train on,” in one sitting.

To make the underlying decoding problem tangible for a general audience (not everyone at a database conference has a quantum information background), I also built QEC Tiles: Stabilizer Rush, a small browser game where you play the decoder in real time.

Paper, abstract, and PDF are on the publications page (Patwardhan et al., 2026).
entry.summary: Why AI-based QEC decoders are starved for data, and how QEC lake fixes that.
